en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Jewel Chapter 90.
The Training Rule on the Itch-Covering Cloth.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had authorized an itch-covering cloth for the monks.
The group of six monks,
thinking, "The Blessed One has authorized an itch-covering cloth," wore itch-covering cloths of unlimited size.
They wander about dragging [the robes] from both the front and the back.
Those monks who have few desires... [as before]... they grumble, complain, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks wear itch-covers of unlimited size?"... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that you wear unlimited itch-covers?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you wear itch-covers of unlimited size?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Now, when a monk is having an itch-covering cloth made, it should be made according to the proper measure.
Herein, this is the measure: four spans in length according to the Sugata-span, and two spans across.
For one who exceeds that, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting down.”
"An itch-covering cloth" means:
for one who has an itch, a boil, a discharge, or severe scabies, or some other ailment below the navel and above the kneecaps, it is for the purpose of covering that.
"By having it made" means...
Whether making it oneself or having it made, it should be made according to the proper measure.
Herein, this is the measure: four spans in length, using the span of the Sugata; two spans across.
If one makes it or has it made exceeding that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of undertaking.
Having cut it after obtaining [the material], one must confess a *pācittiya* offense.
If one brings to completion what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one brings to completion what was begun by oneself through others, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If she brings to completion what has been half-finished by others, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she brings to completion what has been half-finished by others through the agency of others, there is an offense of expiation.
If she makes it for another’s purpose or causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one receives and uses what has been made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if one makes it according to the proper measure.
He makes it deficient;
or, having obtained something made by another that exceeds the prescribed measure, he cuts it down and uses it;
or he makes a canopy, a floor-covering, a screen-wall, a mattress, or a pillow.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The eighth training rule concerning the covering of itch is finished.
